text: A second fictional case study: Brightfield Outfitters launches a customer-facing chatbot, and open-ended generative output creates a different governance problem than last lesson's.

The chatbot's system prompt explicitly declines questions outside its scope, outputs get filtered before customers see them, and its model card states upfront that it can produce fluent, wrong answers about specific orders. The limitation is documented before launch, not discovered by a customer first.

Likelihood of a bad output is scored medium-high — generative text is less predictable than a scoring model. Impact is medium — wrong advice is recoverable, unlike a denied loan. The tier lands lower than Harrow Peak's credit model, but still high enough to require active monitoring.

Three weeks in, the bot confidently states a wrong return-window policy, and it circulates online. Incident response triages it, patches the exact prompt pattern that caused it, fixes affected customers, and logs it into the model's own documentation — not minimized, used as a lesson.
Credit decisioning gets pre-certified; generative text gets boundaries and fast correction instead. Final lesson: actually building an AI governance program from everything this course has covered.
